paras: The Carbon Iron Works strike against Black puddlers was a walkout by the employees of the Carbon Iron Works in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on 4 August 1890, called after the company put Black men to work in its idle puddling department. Between 300 and 500 men left the works, and wire reports said the strikers threatened violence against the Black workers. Papers across the country carried the story as a strike caused by the hiring of "negroes" or "colored men."

The puddlers at the works had been out since about 1 July, when the firm refused to sign the Amalgamated Association's scale of $5 a ton. According to a Pittsburgh wire report, 96 puddlers quit after being offered $4.65, and the firm later offered $4.75 without reaching agreement. When word spread on 3 August that the strikers' places had been filled, employees met at the forks of Butler street and Penn avenue and named a committee of two men from each department to act if the rumor proved true.

On the morning of 4 August, eight of the sixteen graphite furnaces were started with Black men "secured from various places," and the committee at once ordered a general strike. The other departments finished their heats and went home, and by two o'clock the works were idle. One wire version put the Black workforce at 48 men, with 60 more expected from Tennessee, and said the strikers would not work with what they called "black legs."

The same version said the Black workers were "frightened almost out of their wits" because the workmen were making threats of violence, and the Savannah Morning News printed that "threats of bodily harm are made." No assault on the Black workers is reported in the coverage, and the Pittsburg Dispatch's own reports do not mention threats.

On 5 August the Black men kept eight furnaces running while the rest of the plant stayed shut. The general manager said the plant would reopen after two weeks of repairs and that "he would find help where he could," while district vice president Florence Sullivan told a strikers' meeting in Hoecker's Hall to be moderate but hold out.

By 9 August the works ran with non-union men, guarded by special officers and three Black watchmen the company had hired against outside interference. That night one of the watchmen, Richard Herndon, fired at Daniel Sullivan, an 18-year-old fleeing police after a drinking party in a nearby lumber yard; the watchmen said they had taken the noise for an attack on the works. Sullivan died, and a coroner's jury found that he was killed by a gunshot wound at Herndon's hands "with felonious intent," sending Herndon to jail to await the grand jury.

The Pittsburg Dispatch headed its first report "ANOTHER IRON WORKS STRIKE" and explained that the employees quit "Because of Colored Puddlers," treating the walkout as a sympathy strike in a wage dispute. Its labor column the same day carried the deck "The Carbon Iron Works Employs Colored Men, and a Strike Ensues," and its follow-up dealt only with furnaces, repairs and union meetings.

Two wire versions ran on 5 August: one with the scale figures in the Wheeling Register, the Wilmington Evening Journal and the Fairhaven Herald in Washington state, and one stressing the 48 "negroes" and the threats in the Washington Evening Star and the Savannah Morning News. The Savannah paper's headline called it "An Attempt to Put Negroes in the Place of Strikers Resented." Digest items followed in the Freeland Tribune and the Wilmington Delaware Gazette on 7 August and the Martinsburg Herald on 9 August, and the Martinsburg Herald printed the threats version as late as 16 August.
The Cleveland Gazette, an Afro-American weekly, carried a single sentence on 9 August reporting that all 500 employes struck "because Negro puddlers were hired," without comment.

Accounts differ on the size of the walkout: the Wheeling Register's wire copy counted 300 men in the finishing department, while the Evening Star and Savannah Morning News reported 500. They also give different wage figures for the puddlers' original dispute, from a demand of $5 against last year's $4.50 to a demand for 35 cents more a ton.

bases: White workers at the Carbon Iron Works struck to force out 48 Black men hired to fill strikers' places in the puddling department, with reported threats of violence but no reported assault (A1, A4, A6).

The local Pittsburg Dispatch and two separate wire versions agree that the works struck when furnaces were started with Black men (A1, A3, A4, A6); the threats are reported only in the two wire versions (A4, A6).

accounts.label: Pittsburg Dispatch (local)
accounts.gist: The men in the other departments quit in sympathy with the puddlers, whose places were filled by colored men; local union officials ordered the mill struck. No violence or threats are mentioned.

accounts.label: Wire report (300 version)
accounts.gist: A committee of two men per department ordered a general strike as soon as eight of the sixteen furnaces were started with colored men 'secured from various places'; no threats mentioned.

accounts.label: Wire report (500 version)
accounts.gist: Five hundred men struck because 48 negroes were put in the puddling department; the strikers would not work with 'black legs' and were making threats of violence against the frightened Black workers.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette
accounts.gist: A one-line item reported that all 500 employes struck because Negro puddlers were hired.

framing.detail: The Pittsburg Dispatch treated it as one more iron-works wage strike ('ANOTHER IRON WORKS STRIKE'), explaining the Amalgamated scale dispute and saying nothing of threats.
Wire copy ran from Washington to Savannah to Washington state, the longer version stressing the strikers' threats and their refusal to work with 'black legs', the shorter one the scale dispute.
The Afro-American Cleveland Gazette carried only a one-sentence news item without comment.

conflicts.note: The 300 figure is given for the finishing department in A3; the 500 figure for all departments. Neither local report gives a total.

record_check.record: Crowds made threats, escorted and questioned Black men approaching the works, and a white striker fought a Black man.
record_check.dossier: Only threats of violence are reported (wire, A4, A6); no article found reports crowds escorting or questioning Black men or a fight between a striker and a Black man.
threat and work_action only; no beating reported.
